Thiruvananthapuram: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued rain alerts for all 14 districts in Kerala, warning of continued heavy rainfall across the state on Monday.
An orange alert has been issued in Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Malappuram, Ernakulam, Idukki, Kottayam, Alappuzha, and Pathanamthitta, while Palakkad, Thrissur, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram remain under a yellow alert.
According to the weather agency, isolated heavy rainfall accompanied by gusty winds reaching speeds of up to 60 kmph is likely across the state.
With water levels in major rivers continuing to rise, authorities have urged residents in coastal and low-lying areas to remain extremely vigilant. The threat of landslides also persists in hilly regions, with residents in vulnerable locations being advised to relocate to safer grounds.
Advertisement
Meanwhile, district collectors have declared a holiday for all educational institutions in 12 districts due to the prevailing heavy rain in the state.
The holiday applies to all educational institutions, including professional colleges, in Kasaragod, Kannur, Wayanad, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Palakkad, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Idukki, Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Alappuzha.
Advertisement
The ban on fishing also continues as rough sea conditions persist. Fishing has been prohibited along the Kerala, Karnataka and Lakshadweep coasts.
Heavy rains have lashed several parts of the state, triggering landslides and flooding in low-lying areas. In Pathanamthitta, the water level has increased in Ranni, which was recently hit by a flash flood following heavy rain in the district.
With the Moozhiyar Dam catchment area under a Red Alert, authorities have warned that the dam may be opened at any time if conditions worsen. Consequently, the district administration has urged residents living along the banks of the Pamba river to remain extremely vigilant and be prepared to move to safer locations.
According to Kerala Tourism Minister PC Vishnunadh, warnings of extremely heavy rainfall had been accurate, as a result of which the opening of the dam shutters was later revised to 15 cm from 30 cm. The Minister stated that it would take approximately four hours for rainwater from the upper reaches to reach downstream areas.
The Minister further announced that three tipper trucks have been sent to Thiruvalla for rescue operations, adding that more people are currently staying in relief camps in the region.
Additionally, 14 fishing boats will be deployed to strengthen rescue efforts. The Minister stated that an emergency meeting of Revenue Department officials will also be convened in the state.
Meanwhile, eight people have died, eight others remain missing, and thirteen people have sustained injuries in rain-related incidents across the state. Around 5,792 people have been shifted to 209 relief camps set up across Kerala.
According to an official release, Chief Minister VD Satheesan continues to remain in touch with the ministers in charge of various districts and district administrations regarding the rain-related situation in the state.
Additionally, twenty-seven houses have been destroyed while 196 houses have suffered partial damage.
The government said assistance would be provided to the families of those who lost their lives as well as to those who have lost their homes and livelihoods.
The state government has said it is fully prepared to deal with any emergency situation and urged people to strictly follow the instructions issued by the government and district administrations.

Kerala continues to battle heavy rainfall, with the death toll from rain-related incidents rising to 15 by Sunday night. Malappuram reported the highest number of fatalities with four deaths, followed by Thiruvananthapuram, Kottayam and Idukki with two each, while one person died in Kozhikode.
Thousands shifted to relief camps
The state government said 7674 people have been moved to 273 relief camps across Kerala. The incessant rain has completely destroyed 30 houses and damaged another 293. Although rainfall eased on Sunday, several towns in central Kerala remain waterlogged, disrupting daily life and causing extensive property damage.
Orange Alert in 10 districts
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an Orange Alert for Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Idukki, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod. Authorities have also declared a holiday for schools, colleges, anganwadis, tuition centres, training institutes and madrasas in several affected districts. Meanwhile, a Red Alert has been issued for Kallarkutty, Pambla, Erattayar and Kallar dams.
River alerts and emergency review
The State Irrigation Department has issued Orange and Yellow alerts for several rivers after water levels rose sharply. People living near riverbanks have been urged to remain alert, avoid entering rivers and shift from flood-prone areas if advised by authorities.
Chief Minister VD Satheesan convened an emergency meeting of district collectors, senior officials and ministers on Monday morning to review the flood situation, relief camp operations, rescue efforts and preparedness. articles.full_text:
The India Meteorological Department has escalated its weather warnings across Keralam, issuing an urgent 'Orange' alert for 12 districts as torrential downpours continue to batter the southern Indian state, triggering severe landslides and forcing mass evacuations.
The intensifying monsoon systems threaten to cripple regional infrastructure and agricultural output, presenting immediate supply chain risks that stretch from local spice markets in Kochi to import hubs across East Africa, including Kenya's Port of Mombasa. The severe weather event underscores the escalating volatility of regional climate patterns, demanding urgent adaptive strategies from disaster management authorities.
Extensive Geographic Impact and Evacuations
According to the latest India Meteorological Department bulletins, the heightened 'Orange' alert encompasses Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Idukki, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur, and Kasaragod districts. Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam remain under a 'Yellow' alert. The widespread nature of the severe weather warning indicates a systemic atmospheric disturbance capable of generating catastrophic localized flooding.
State authorities have rapidly mobilized disaster response protocols. District collectors across the 12 heavily impacted regions have mandated the immediate closure of all educational institutions, prioritizing civilian safety amid deteriorating road conditions. Rescue operations are currently underway in vulnerable topographical zones, particularly in the hilly terrains of Idukki and Wayanad, which remain highly susceptible to fatal mudslides.
Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan confirmed that multiple fatalities have already been recorded, with ongoing search and rescue missions attempting to locate individuals missing in debris flows. Authorities have established over 200 emergency relief camps, providing shelter to nearly 6,000 displaced residents across the state.
Infrastructure and Agricultural Devastation
The relentless precipitation has fundamentally compromised critical infrastructure. Peerumade and Thodupuzha taluks have recorded excess rainfall exceeding 200 millimetres, accelerating structural damage to rural housing and tertiary road networks. Over 200 homes have sustained partial or complete structural failure.
The agricultural sector faces profound disruption. Kerala, a globally significant producer of cardamom, black pepper, and natural rubber, anticipates severe crop damage. Waterlogged plantations risk root rot, threatening to diminish harvest yields for the upcoming fiscal quarter. This disruption presents immediate economic ramifications for thousands of smallholder farming cooperatives dependent on predictable weather cycles.
Key infrastructure vulnerabilities include:
- Reservoir Capacities: Catchment areas, including the Moozhiyar Dam, are operating near maximum capacity, necessitating controlled water releases that further inundate downstream communities along the Pamba River.
- Maritime Operations: Authorities have implemented a strict prohibition on all fishing activities along the Kerala, Karnataka, and Lakshadweep coastlines due to sustained wind speeds reaching 60 kilometres per hour.
- Transportation Networks: Mountainous ghat thoroughfares face severe restrictions, with night travel explicitly discouraged to prevent vehicular accidents amid sudden landslips.
Global Supply Chain and Diaspora Implications
The climatic disruptions in Kerala generate tangible economic ripples far beyond the Indian subcontinent. For East African economies, particularly Kenya, the implications are directly measurable. Kenya imports substantial volumes of Indian agricultural commodities and pharmaceuticals; any sustained disruption at major maritime hubs like the Port of Cochin inevitably translates to delayed shipments arriving at Mombasa.
Furthermore, the crisis activates intense concern within the global Keralite diaspora. Remittances from expatriates working in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations, the United Kingdom, and African economic centres form a critical pillar of Kerala's gross domestic product. Diaspora communities are currently mobilizing emergency relief funds, navigating complex currency conversions to transmit financial aid—often measured in millions of US Dollars (equivalent to billions of Kenyan Shillings).
Disaster Preparedness and Policy Frameworks
The current flooding crisis exposes persistent vulnerabilities in the state's disaster forecasting and rapid response mechanisms. While the deployment of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) demonstrates centralized coordination, the localized devastation reveals the urgent need for hyper-granular meteorological tracking.
Environmental experts point to unchecked ecological degradation in the fragile Western Ghats as a primary catalyst for the increasing frequency of lethal landslides. The systemic removal of deep-rooted vegetation for commercial development continues to destabilize hillside topsoil, creating perfect conditions for catastrophic debris flows during intense monsoon deluges.
As state agencies race to fortify riverbanks and evacuate high-risk zones, the immediate priority remains the preservation of human life amid highly unpredictable weather systems. The unfolding situation in Kerala serves as a stark metric of climate vulnerability, demanding structural reforms in how developing regions engineer resilience against increasingly extreme atmospheric events.

articles.full_text:
A catastrophic weather system has plunged the southern Indian state of Kerala into a severe humanitarian crisis. As relentless torrential rains batter the coastal region, state disaster management authorities have confirmed that at least eight people have died, with an equal number reported missing beneath mudslides and surging floodwaters.
The situation escalated rapidly on Monday, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue an emergency Orange Alert across 12 of the state's 14 districts. In Pathanamthitta and Wayanad, rivers have breached their banks, inundating entire townships and severing vital logistical corridors. Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan's administration has mobilized emergency response units, promising immediate financial and infrastructural aid to families whose livelihoods have been washed away.
The Anatomy of the Disaster
The intensity of the current monsoon system has overwhelmed Kerala's natural and engineered drainage infrastructure. The destruction is characterized by dual threats: rapid urban waterlogging in the lowlands and devastating landslides in the fragile Western Ghats.
Field reports from emergency responders detail a highly volatile environment where rescue operations are continuously hampered by poor visibility and unstable terrain.
- Casualty Metrics: Official logs from the Chief Minister's Office (CMO) confirm 8 fatalities, with search operations ongoing for 8 individuals trapped in landslide debris.
- Displacement Data: Thousands of residents have been forcibly evacuated from low-lying areas, seeking shelter in 27 active government relief camps.
- Infrastructure Collapse: Arterial roads in Pathanamthitta have been completely submerged, while electrical grids in the high ranges have suffered catastrophic failures due to uprooted vegetation.
Climate Volatility: A Shared Global Reality
The extreme weather events paralyzing Kerala are not isolated geographical anomalies; they are explicit indicators of accelerating global climate volatility. The atmospheric patterns dumping unprecedented rainfall on the Malabar Coast share a direct meteorological lineage with the climate crises devastating the African continent.
In May 2024, Kenya experienced horrific, anomalous flooding driven by the El Niño weather phenomenon. Entire settlements in Mai Mahiu were obliterated by flash floods, and the Tana River basin was transformed into an inland sea, displacing hundreds of thousands. The structural challenges faced by the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) in predicting localized super-storms are identical to the hurdles faced by India's IMD. Both regions are discovering that legacy urban planning and traditional agricultural cycles are fundamentally unequipped to survive the new era of hyper-concentrated rainfall.
Whether it is the destruction of coffee plantations in Wayanad or the ruin of maize crops in the Rift Valley, the economic shockwaves of these localized disasters eventually register on global commodity markets.
The Failure of the Western Ghats
Environmental scientists have repeatedly warned that the death toll in Kerala is not solely an act of nature, but the result of aggressive ecological degradation. The Western Ghats, a UNESCO World Heritage site, have been systematically compromised by illegal quarrying, unregulated resort construction, and the destruction of deep-rooted native vegetation.
"When you replace ancient shola forests with concrete and monoculture plantations, the mountains lose their ability to act as a sponge," explains Dr. Thomas Varghese, an environmental geologist. "The soil reaches saturation within hours of heavy rain, liquefies, and brings the entire hillside down onto the settlements below. This is exactly what we are witnessing in Chooralmala and Pathanamthitta today."
Mobilizing for Survival
As the Orange Alert remains active, the immediate focus is on preservation of life. The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), alongside local police and volunteer networks, is engaged in high-risk extractions in the most isolated pockets of the state.
However, the recurring nature of Kerala's floods—echoing the historic devastation of 2018—demands a radical reimagining of disaster resilience. Providing post-disaster compensation is no longer a viable long-term strategy. The state must urgently enforce strict ecological zoning laws, dismantle structures in high-risk landslide corridors, and invest heavily in early-warning telemetry.
For the thousands currently huddled in relief camps listening to the unending rain, the promise of government aid offers cold comfort. They are on the frontline of a climate war that is rewriting the geography of their homeland, demanding absolute adaptation if they are to survive the next monsoon.

Delhi Weather LATEST Update: Rain, Thunderstorms Likely Across NCR; IMD Issues Yellow Alert for Tuesday
Delhi Weather LATEST Update: Delhi-NCR woke up to cloudy skies and sticky weather on Monday, with the India Meteorological Department forecasting light rain in several parts of the region. More widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected
Cloudy Monday, Rain to Build Across Delhi-NCR
Delhi and the neighbouring NCR cities are expected to witness a cloudy day with light rainfall, offering some respite from the humid weather. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), scattered showers are likely in Delhi, while Noida could experience multiple spells of rain and Gurugram may receive one or two showers through the day.
Temperatures are expected to remain comfortable compared to recent days, ranging between 24°C and 33°C in Delhi. However, high humidity levels will continue to make conditions feel uncomfortable despite the moderate temperatures.
Tuesday May Bring Stronger Showers and Thunderstorms
Weather conditions are expected to become more active from Tuesday, when the IMD has issued a yellow alert for Delhi. Widespread rain and thunderstorms are likely across several parts of the NCR, with Noida and surrounding eastern areas having a greater chance of receiving repeated showers.
Rainfall is expected to remain uneven across the region. While some localities could receive heavy downpours within a short period, nearby areas may witness only light rain or remain largely dry. Cloudy skies and intermittent rainfall are likely to continue through much of the week.
Rain and Kanwar Traffic Restrictions Could Slow Commuters
The expected rainfall may coincide with the evening rush hour, increasing the chances of traffic congestion across Delhi-NCR. Waterlogging on vulnerable roads could further slow movement, particularly on busy routes such as the DND Flyway, Noida-Greater Noida Expressway and roads connecting east Delhi with Noida.
Travel may become more challenging as Kanwar Yatra traffic restrictions remain in place across parts of Delhi, Ghaziabad and connecting highways. Commuters are advised to plan their journeys in advance, especially if travelling through the Delhi-Meerut corridor or other diversion routes.

Assam CM Himanta Biswa Sarma visited flood-hit Sivasagar to review relief measures. He announced a Rs 112 crore interim package for affected families and confirmed significant progress in restoring power infrastructure in the district.
CM Sarma Reviews Flood Situation in Sivasagar
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Monday visited the flood-affected Nepalikhuti area in Sivasagar district to assess the prevailing situation and review the relief and rehabilitation measures being undertaken by the administration.
During the visit, the Chief Minister interacted with flood-affected residents, heard their concerns, and took stock of the damage caused by the floods. He also reviewed the ongoing relief operations and directed officials to ensure timely assistance to all affected families.
Accompanied by Assam Minister Pijush Hazarika and senior officials from the district administration, Chief Minister Sarma surveyed the flood-damaged zones near the Assam-Nagaland border, where deluge waters caused extensive loss to life, property, and agricultural livelihoods.
Relief and Compensation Measures
During his visit, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma personally interacted with affected families at relief camps, assessing their immediate needs for food, drinking water, medical assistance, and compensation for lost livestock and submerged homes.
"We stand firmly with every flood-affected family during this critical time. The state government has already initiated the distribution of interim relief to affected households across Dibrugarh, Sivasagar, and adjoining areas. Our immediate focus is to ensure that relief camps maintain uninterrupted supplies of food, clean drinking water, and essential healthcare services", the CM said.
"While floodwaters are receding, the extent of damage, especially due to mud, silt, and damaged homes, remains significant. District Commissioners have been directed to conduct a comprehensive assessment of crop destruction, livestock loss, and house damage so that appropriate compensation can be sanctioned without delay. The Central and State governments have sufficient resources, and we will rebuild affected livelihoods on a priority basis", he added.
Minister Pijush Hazarika also reviewed the initiatives taken by the Water Resources and Agriculture Departments to support impacted farmers and reinforce embankments along vulnerable river stretches in Demow and Nazira constituencies.
"Our priority right now is ensuring immediate relief, clean drinking water, and food supplies to every affected household in Nepalikhuti and surrounding areas. The Chief Minister has strictly directed all district officials and department heads to expedite the damage assessment process so that compensation for lost crops, submerged homes, and livestock can be sanctioned without delay. The Water Resources Department is also taking emergency measures to repair and reinforce breached embankments on a war footing to prevent further damage", he told reporters here.
Significant Progress in Power Restoration
In a major relief for flood-affected residents in Upper Assam, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Monday reported significant progress in restoring power infrastructure across Sivasagar district.
Encouraging progress on power restoration. Over the last 24 hours, our teams have safely reconnected many more transformers, bringing down the number of affected consumers in Sivasagar by nearly 58%. We are steadily moving towards full normalisation of the power situation. https://t.co/4uXMoNN7jo pic.twitter.com/91OjcXYCG3 — Himanta Biswa Sarma (@himantabiswa) August 3, 2026
Taking to X, Chief Minister Sarma stated that electricity teams have successfully reconnected numerous transformers over the past 24 hours, leading to a sharp drop in power disruptions across affected localities.
"Encouraging progress on power restoration. Over the last 24 hours, our teams have safely reconnected many more transformers, bringing down the number of affected consumers in Sivasagar by nearly 58%. We are steadily moving towards full normalisation of the power situation," CM Himanta Biswa Sarma said on X.
Financial Aid and Infrastructure Support
Earlier, Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Monday rolled out an interim flood-relief package worth nearly Rs 112 crore, transferring financial assistance directly into the bank accounts of around 75,000 affected families across four districts.
Addressing beneficiaries who joined virtually from Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat, CM Sarma confirmed that each eligible household received an immediate grant of Rs 15,000 via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). The state-wide disbursement drive is scheduled to continue through August 5.
In addition to family relief, the Chief Minister announced an infrastructure support fund of Rs 2 lakh each for flood-damaged schools and Anganwadi centres across the affected regions.
Subsidies under the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana were also distributed to local recipients during the event at the CM Secretariat in Dibrugarh. (ANI)
